name: Omar Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself and how you came to line work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: For fifteen years I was a rigger in the concert business, hanging lights and speakers from arena roofs, so heights were never the problem. The problem was being away 200 nights a year while Priya raised the kids. At 41 I joined a contractor that builds new power lines for the electricity company, mostly connecting solar farms, wind farms and these huge data centres to the grid. Priya's a pharmacist, and we've got Zaid, who's eleven, and Noor, who's eight. We bought a little flat back in my touring days and rent it out, which is a big part of why we're comfortable.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now we're building a new line out to a solar farm past the ring road, about forty steel poles across fields. I'm usually on the ground crew with Luis, assembling cross-arms and insulators, feeding cable, and going up in the bucket with Ruth, our foreman, when she lets me. I still make rookie mistakes, like last week I torqued a bolt to the wrong setting and Ruth made me redo the whole arm. I use an AI app on the drive in to quiz me on the bits I'm weak on, which the older guys laugh at. I love building something new that wasn't there in the morning, and what wears me out is the mud, honestly, and being the slowest on the crew after years of being the expert at my old job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, I was wrong, the hype people were wrong, let's get on with it. I'd probably post something about how the grid still needed building anyway, because the solar farms don't connect themselves. At work Luis would rib me for weeks about my quiz app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed. I like this stuff, I think the tools are genuinely clever, and I'd hoped they'd take the boring paperwork off us. But for my family it's good news, because the job stays the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying for my ticket, keep using the tools for what they're good at, which is quizzing me and writing up my site diary. We'd keep putting the flat rent into savings. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AI Plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little let down. It's like buying a new drill that turns out to be the same as the old one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss, if the tools stayed this small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hoped one day you'd point a camera at a pole and it'd tell you exactly what's wrong and how to fix it safely. That would help a junior like me a lot. Without it, I'm learning the old way, from Ruth shouting at me, which honestly works too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do the older guys on the crew use any of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth uses it to sort the rotas, though she'd never admit it. Luis won't touch it, says if it can't hold a shovel he doesn't want to know. So it's a split crew, really.

S0.say: He'd admit the hype was wrong and post that the grid still needed building anyway. At work he'd put up with weeks of ribbing about his quiz app.
S0.think: He'd be a bit disappointed, because he likes the tools and hoped they'd take paperwork off the crew. For his family it's good news because the job stays the same.
S0.do: Keeps studying for his ticket and using AI for quizzing and his site diary. Keeps putting the flat's rent into savings without any big change.
S0.feel: Calm and a little let down.
S0.quote: It's like buying a new drill that turns out to be the same as the old one.
S0.fieldNote: Omar is the rare lineworker who'd be disappointed by the plateau, because he enjoys the tools. His security comes from the rented flat and Priya's job. He reads his crew as split on technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when unions matter most, because change is coming whether we like it or not, and the question is who gets the benefit. I'd push our branch to get training written into the contract: if the company brings in new tools, every worker gets paid time to learn them. Online I'd share stuff about how the grid is booming because of AI, ironically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a decent spot. The data centres need power, so contractors like ours will be busy for years, and I'm the one on the crew who's comfortable with the tech. If drones start doing inspections or software plans the routes, I can be the guy who knows how it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ruth if I could be on any trial of new kit, drones, smart tools, whatever comes. I'd take an evening course on drone flying, because I reckon line inspection by drone will be big. And I'd go to the union meetings and push for that training clause, because I don't want Luis left behind just because he hates screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing Steady Disruption?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually, maybe even a bit excited. It's change I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want Luis left behind. What would happen to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis is 50 and the best ground man I've met, he can read a field and tell you where the soft ground is just by walking it. But if the paperwork goes onto tablets and he refuses, management will find a reason to push him out. I'd rather sit with him at lunch and show him the basics than watch that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The data centres themselves, a bit. We're building lines to feed machines that might take Priya's job one day, checking prescriptions and all that. That's a strange thing to think about while you're bolting on insulators.

S1.say: He'd say unions matter most now and push his branch to write paid training time into the contract. Online he'd point out the irony that AI is driving a grid boom.
S1.think: He thinks he's in a decent spot: data centres keep contractors busy and he's the crew member comfortable with tech. He could become the one who knows how the new tools work.
S1.do: Asks to join any trial of new kit and takes an evening course in drone flying for line inspection. Pushes the training clause at union meetings and plans to help Luis with tablets at lunch.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, because it's change he can work with.
S1.quote: We're building lines to feed machines that might take Priya's job one day, checking prescriptions and all that.
S1.fieldNote: Omar sees opportunity and moves first, but his progressive streak shows in wanting colleagues brought along. The irony of feeding data centres that might hit his partner's job wasn't lost on him. Luis is the colleague he'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this has to be shared, or it's going to be ugly. The robots will be working a grid that public money and our sweat built, so the public should own a slice. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd be writing to our local representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think even being good with the tech won't save me with only two years. I'm a junior with three years in the trade, and the robot will be better than me by the time I qualify. But we've got the flat and Priya's wage, at least at first, so it's more about what I do with myself than whether we eat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ask the company to put me on the team that sets up and supervises the robots, because someone has to bring them out to site and check them, at least for a while. I'd keep the flat rent going into savings and stop any big spending. And I'd join whatever campaign started for a public share of AI profits, because that's the only fix that's big enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm usually the one telling people not to worry, so this feels strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having just two years change things for you, compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means no long plan works. I'd be trying to jump onto the robot team, but so would everyone else who likes gadgets, and there'd be maybe one of those jobs for every ten of us. With more years I could build a real skill, but with two I'm grabbing at whatever's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Zaid and Noor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zaid would actually be excited, he's into robots, he'd want to see one climb a pole. Noor would ask if Daddy's going back on tour, because that's all she remembers about my old job. I'd tell her no, Daddy's staying home either way, and that's a promise.

S2.say: He'd say loudly that AGI has to be shared, since the robots will work a grid built with public money and workers' sweat. He'd go to every union meeting and write to his local representative.
S2.think: He thinks being good with tech won't save a junior with three years in the trade when there are only two years. The flat and Priya's wage mean the question is purpose more than food.
S2.do: Asks to join the team that sets up and supervises the robots on site. Keeps saving the flat's rent, stops big spending, and joins a campaign for a public share of AI profits.
S2.feel: Anxious, which feels strange for someone who usually tells others not to worry.
S2.quote: There'd be maybe one of those jobs for every ten of us.
S2.fieldNote: Even an early adopter sees limits when the timeline is two years. His plan to join the robot team is sensible but he admits competition would be fierce. The promise to Noor that he won't go back on tour shows what he values most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do it right if we start tomorrow. I'd be pushing for a deal at work where the company trains its own lineworkers to run the robots, instead of hiring in tech people from outside. Online I'd probably share stuff about countries or companies doing it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to qualify and become the go-to guy on the new kit. I could see myself as a sort of robot crew lead, the person who knows the line work and the machine. It's not forever, but it's another five or ten years of good work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify as fast as I can, and I'd do a proper course in robotics maintenance at the technical college at night, maybe two evenings a week for a couple of years. I'd use the AI tools even more, to learn the robot manuals before anyone else has read them. We'd keep saving, and maybe sell the flat at the right time and put it into something less tied to our town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than worried. Five years feels like a race I could actually run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said sell the flat. Why would you sell it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AGI is coming, I'm not sure who'll be renting a one-bed above a high street in seven years. I'd rather turn it into savings or shares in a broad fund. It's the one big thing we own that's tied to the town staying the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked about collective action and also about racing ahead yourself. Are those in tension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. I want everyone to be OK, and I also want to be first in line. I suppose I think if I'm on the robot team, I can help get Luis and the others in too, but maybe that's just me telling myself a nice story.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to do it right if they start now, and push for the company to train its own lineworkers to run the robots instead of hiring outsiders.
S3.think: He thinks five years lets him qualify and become the go-to person on new kit, a kind of robot crew lead who knows both the line and the machine, for another five or ten years.
S3.do: Qualifies fast and studies robotics maintenance at the technical college two evenings a week. Uses AI to learn the robot manuals early, keeps saving and considers selling the flat for a broad fund.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more curious than worried, like a race he could actually run.
S3.quote: I want everyone to be OK, and I also want to be first in line.
S3.fieldNote: When I named the tension between solidarity and racing ahead, he owned it with real honesty. His plan to sell the rental flat shows clear thinking about local assets. Five years turns fear into a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a proper window, and we should use it for a national retraining plan, a shorter working week, and a public stake in the robot fleets. I'd be pretty vocal about it, probably too vocal for some of my mates. At work I'd keep it light and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well out of ten years. I'd qualify, I'd get good, and I'd move into the robot side by year five. By 2036 I'd be 53, and with the flat and our savings I wouldn't be panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd plan it out in steps: qualify by year two, drone and robotics training by year four, and apply for any supervisor or trainer role on the new kit after that. I'd move some of our savings into a fund that includes the companies making the robots, so we're not just on the losing side. And I'd get really involved in the union's tech committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of buzz. Ten years is enough to choose, not just react.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd invest in the companies making the robots. Does that sit right with your politics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not completely. But I'd rather own a sliver of the thing and push for it to be shared than stand outside shouting with nothing. Priya says I'm trying to have it both ways, and she's probably right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Zaid and Noor by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zaid will be 21, Noor 18. I'd want them doing something with people, not something a machine does better. Honestly I don't know what that is yet, and I'd tell them I don't know.

S4.say: He'd call ten years a proper window for a national retraining plan, a shorter working week and a public stake in robot fleets. He'd keep it practical at work but be vocal elsewhere.
S4.think: He thinks he'd do well with ten years: qualify, get good, move to the robot side by year five, and reach 53 with the flat and savings behind him.
S4.do: Plans to qualify by year two and train in drones and robotics by year four, then apply for supervisor or trainer roles on the new kit. Moves some savings into a fund that includes robot makers and joins the union's tech committee.
S4.feel: Calm with a bit of buzz, because ten years lets him choose.
S4.quote: I'd rather own a sliver of the thing and push for it to be shared than stand outside shouting with nothing.
S4.fieldNote: Omar is at ease with a decade and has a staged plan. His investing in robot makers sits uneasily with his politics, and he admits it, quoting his partner. He's honest that he doesn't know what to advise his kids.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Even for someone like me who likes the tech, two years means there's no ladder to climb, just a scramble for a few jobs. What would help is a proper public deal: lineworkers trained to run the robots on paid time, and some share of the profits going back to the people whose jobs went.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who build the infrastructure for all this. We're out in the mud laying the lines that power the data centres. It's a strange feeling, building the thing that might replace you, and I don't think many people outside the trade realise that's what we're doing.

headlineQuote: It's a strange feeling, building the thing that might replace you, and I don't think many people outside the trade realise that's what we're doing.
portrait: Omar Abbott is a 43-year-old junior lineworker for a contractor that connects solar farms and data centres to the grid, after fifteen years as a concert rigger. He uses AI daily to study, owns a rented flat with his pharmacist partner Priya, and is comfortable with risk. He's calm and even a little disappointed in the plateau, and sees steady change as a chance to become the crew's tech person. Only AGI in two years makes him anxious, because there'd be too few robot-side jobs for everyone. With five or ten years he plans a staged move into robotics, invests in robot makers, and openly admits the tension between solidarity and wanting to be first in line.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because even someone good with technology would face a scramble for a few jobs rather than a ladder to climb.
whatWouldHelp: A public deal where lineworkers are trained on paid time to run the robots, and a share of the profits goes back to people whose jobs went.
